youtube.aciklama:
Why does a hearing aid give different gain to soft and loud sounds? In this lesson we cover the dynamic range, the input-output curve, compression threshold and ratio, WDRC and compression limiting, expansion, and attack and release times.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; ANSI/ASA S3.22, Specification of Hearing Aid Characteristics; Venema, Compression for Clinicians; Gatehouse, Naylor and Elberling, Linear and nonlinear hearing aid fittings, International Journal of Audiology (2006); Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Compression threshold, ratio, attack and release
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn why hearing aids need compression and how to read an input-output curve.
Step by step, we will cover compression threshold, compression ratio, attack and release times, and limiting of maximum output.
In a normal-hearing ear, there is a range of about 100 decibels between the softest audible sound and an uncomfortable sound.
This range is called the dynamic range.
In cochlear loss the threshold rises, but the discomfort level often stays about the same.

cumleler.yazi: In this example, the threshold is 60 and the discomfort level is 100 dB HL, so the dynamic range has shrunk to about 40 decibels.
cumleler.ses: In this example, the threshold is sixty and the discomfort level is one hundred decibels HL, so the dynamic range has shrunk to about forty decibels.

cumleler: This is the result of the abnormally fast growth of loudness that we saw in the recruitment lesson.
The range of everyday sounds, from soft to loud, does not fit into this narrowed space.
Speech, for example, spans about 30 decibels from weak consonants to strong vowels, and its level changes with the setting.
The aim of compression is to fit a wide input range into the person's narrowed dynamic range.
In linear amplification, the aid applies the same gain to every input level.
In this example the gain is 35 decibels: a 50 decibel input becomes 85, and a 70 decibel input becomes a 105 decibel output.
So the input-output curve is a straight line with a slope of one.
The problem is this: if there is enough gain to make soft sounds audible, loud sounds become uncomfortable.
And if there is little enough gain to keep loud sounds comfortable, soft sounds are not heard.
When the output reached the aid's limit, older linear aids cut off the peaks of the wave; this is called peak clipping.
Peak clipping limits the sound but creates marked distortion.
Compression was developed to solve these two problems together.
The best way to understand compression is the input-output curve.
The horizontal axis shows the level of sound entering the aid, and the vertical axis shows the output level measured in the coupler.

cumleler.yazi: In this example, the aid works linearly up to 50 dB SPL and gives 35 decibels of gain.
cumleler.ses: In this example, the aid works linearly up to fifty decibels SPL and gives thirty five decibels of gain.

cumleler: The point where the curve bends is called the compression threshold, or kneepoint.
Above the compression threshold, when the input rises by 20 decibels, the output rises by only 10 decibels.

cumleler.yazi: The ratio of the input change to the output change is called the compression ratio; here it is 2 to 1.
cumleler.ses: The ratio of the input change to the output change is called the compression ratio; here it is two to one.

cumleler: So gain decreases as input rises: the gap between the curve and the dashed line keeps widening.
At the top there is a second bend: here the output hardly rises at all, and maximum output is limited.
In the standard measurement, this curve is plotted from 50 to 90 dB SPL in 5 decibel steps.
When different ratios are compared at the same compression threshold, the slope of the curve changes.

cumleler.yazi: A ratio of 1 to 1 means no compression; the aid works linearly.
cumleler.ses: A ratio of one to one means no compression; the aid works linearly.

cumleler.yazi: At a ratio of 2 to 1, a 20 decibel rise in input becomes a 10 decibel rise in output.
cumleler.ses: At a ratio of two to one, a twenty decibel rise in input becomes a ten decibel rise in output.

cumleler.yazi: At a ratio of 3 to 1, the same rise drops to about 7 decibels; the curve flattens further.
cumleler.ses: At a ratio of three to one, the same rise drops to about seven decibels; the curve flattens further.

cumleler.yazi: At a ratio of 10 to 1 or higher, the output stays almost constant; this is now limiting.
cumleler.ses: At a ratio of ten to one or higher, the output stays almost constant; this is now limiting.

cumleler: So as the ratio grows, the output range narrows and the loudness differences between sounds shrink.
Very high ratios can flatten the natural loudness changes of speech and make sound less natural.
From the input-output curve, we can read the gain at each input level; gain is output minus input.
A soft sound of forty decibels is amplified to 75 decibels; the gain is 35 decibels.
At the compression threshold of 50 decibels, the gain is still 35 decibels.
For a seventy decibel input, the output is 95 decibels; the gain has dropped to 25 decibels.
For a loud input of ninety decibels, the gain is only 15 decibels.
So a 50 decibel input range has been fitted into an output range of only 30 decibels; this is the essence of compression.

cumleler.yazi: Wide dynamic range compression, or WDRC, is the basic operating mode of today's hearing aids.
cumleler.ses: Wide dynamic range compression, or W D R C, is the basic operating mode of today's hearing aids.

cumleler.yazi: In WDRC the compression threshold is low, usually about 40 to 55 dB SPL, at or below the level of soft speech.
cumleler.ses: In W D R C the compression threshold is low, usually about forty to fifty five decibels SPL, at or below the level of soft speech.

cumleler: So most soft, moderate and loud sounds are processed in the compression region.

cumleler.yazi: In WDRC the ratio is usually low; in most fittings it stays below 3 to 1.
cumleler.ses: In W D R C the ratio is usually low; in most fittings it stays below three to one.

cumleler: The aim is to fit sounds into the dynamic range by giving more gain to soft sounds and less to loud sounds.
Compression limiting, by contrast, only acts at a high threshold near the output limit.

cumleler.yazi: Its ratio is high, usually 8 to 1 or more, so the output does not exceed the discomfort level.
cumleler.ses: Its ratio is high, usually eight to one or more, so the output does not exceed the discomfort level.

cumleler.yazi: In short, WDRC places sounds within the person's hearing range, and limiting protects the upper edge of that range.
cumleler.ses: In short, W D R C places sounds within the person's hearing range, and limiting protects the upper edge of that range.

cumleler: There are two ways to limit maximum output: peak clipping and compression limiting.
In peak clipping, the peaks of the wave that exceed the limit are cut off flat.
The clipped wave is no longer a pure sine wave; new harmonics appear and the sound becomes crackly.
In compression limiting, the aid reduces its gain instead; the shape of the wave is kept, and only its amplitude shrinks.
So compression limiting gives a much cleaner sound in loud settings.
Today, peak clipping may still be used in some very powerful aids and as a final safety limit.
If a person complains that loud sounds are crackly, the possibility that the output is clipping should come to mind.

maddeler.metin: Gain drops for very soft inputs
Too much also cuts soft speech

cumleler: Below the compression threshold, for very soft inputs, some aids work in the opposite direction.
In this region, gain decreases as input decreases; this is called expansion.
The aim is to keep the microphone's own noise and faint sounds, such as a refrigerator hum, from being heard in a quiet room.
On the graph, the slope of the curve in the expansion region is greater than one.
But if expansion is set too strongly, soft speech from a distance can also be weakened.
So a real-ear measurement at a soft input level is important to confirm that the expansion setting does not cut speech.
Compression is defined not only by how much it acts, but also by how fast it responds.

cumleler.yazi: In this example, the input level suddenly rises from 55 to 90 dB SPL.
cumleler.ses: In this example, the input level suddenly rises from fifty five to ninety decibels SPL.

cumleler: Because the aid cannot reduce gain instantly, a brief peak appears in the output, and then the output settles at its new level.
In the standard, attack time is the time after this sudden rise until the output falls to within 3 decibels of its final level.
When the input drops back to 55 decibels, gain does not return at once; the output stays low for a while.
Release time is the time until the output returns to within 4 decibels of its final level.
In most aids the attack time is short, a few milliseconds, so sudden loud sounds are controlled quickly.
Release time varies widely between aids and determines the character of compression.
The standard makes these measurements at the frequencies where the input-output curve is measured.
Compression with a short release time, below about 200 milliseconds, is called fast or syllabic compression.
This type of compression can change gain even between the syllables of speech.
Its advantage is that a weak consonant right after a strong vowel also gets enough gain to be heard.
Its disadvantage is that it flattens the natural envelope of speech and raises the background in noise, making the sound seem to pump.
Compression with release times from hundreds of milliseconds to several seconds is called slow compression.
Slow compression adjusts gain to the overall sound level of the setting and behaves like an automatic volume control.
Its advantage is that it preserves the envelope and naturalness of speech.
Its disadvantage is that after a sudden loud sound, such as a door slamming, soft sounds are under-amplified for a while.
Studies suggest that which approach is more helpful may vary from person to person.
Some research has linked this difference to the person's cognitive capacity, but there is no single rule in the clinic.

maddeler.metin: Each channel has its own threshold, ratio
Low and high frequencies processed separately
Prescriptions give targets for three inputs

cumleler: Today's hearing aids split sound into several frequency channels and apply separate compression in each one.
So each channel can have its own compression threshold and ratio.
This lets compression be set by frequency for a person who hears better at low frequencies and worse at high frequencies.
We will cover channels and bands in detail in the next lesson.
To set compression, prescriptive formulas give separate targets for soft, moderate and loud input levels.

cumleler.yazi: In real-ear measurement, results close to target for 55, 65 and 80 dB SPL inputs show that compression is set correctly.
cumleler.ses: In real-ear measurement, results close to target for fifty five, sixty five and eighty decibel SPL inputs show that compression is set correctly.

cumleler: Matching target at the moderate level alone is not enough; soft and loud levels are also checked separately.

sahneler.metin: For "I can't hear soft sounds", check soft-input gain and expansion; for "loud sounds bother me", check maximum output.
cumleler: A tip from the field: sort compression complaints by input level.
If the person says they cannot hear whispers or distant speech, check the soft-input gain and the expansion setting.
If they say loud sounds are uncomfortable, first review maximum output and limiting.
Complaints that the sound is pumping or fluctuating are often related to a short release time.
After each change, verify the result with a real-ear measurement at the relevant input level.

maddeler.metin: Dynamic range narrows; compression fits sounds
WDRC low threshold, limiting high threshold

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that the dynamic range narrows in cochlear loss and that compression fits sounds into this range.
The compression threshold is the point where the input-output curve bends; the ratio is the input change divided by the output change.

cumleler.yazi: WDRC uses a low threshold and low ratio; compression limiting protects maximum output with a high threshold and high ratio.
cumleler.ses: W D R C uses a low threshold and low ratio; compression limiting protects maximum output with a high threshold and high ratio.

cumleler: Attack time is short; release time separates fast from slow compression.

sahneler.soru: Above threshold, input rises 30 dB, output 10 dB. Ratio?

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: above the compression threshold, the input rises by 30 decibels while the output rises by 10. What is the compression ratio?
The correct answer is C: 3 to 1.
cumleler.ses: The correct answer is C: three to one.

cumleler: The compression ratio is the input change divided by the output change: thirty divided by ten, which is three.
